The path of a connection

Every client connection string names the region's database hostname, a port, and the project's database:

postgresql://blog_k2f9_owner:…@db.example.com:6543/blog_k2f9?sslmode=require
  1. DNS and the floating IP. The hostname points at the region's floating IP. Hetzner routes that address to one of two pooler hosts. Without pooler hosts, the PgBouncers run beside xenibase-server, as in the compose bundle.
  2. PgBouncer. :5432 is session mode, for migrations, LISTEN and anything that needs a session. :6543 is transaction mode, for app traffic, with up to 200 prepared statements tracked per connection. Both run the same configuration (deploy/pgbouncer). TLS is required (client_tls_sslmode = require, TLS 1.2 or 1.3).
  3. Who may log in from where. auth_type = hba: PgBouncer reads the generated hba.conf, then checks the password against the SCRAM verifier in the generated userlist.txt. PgBouncer never sees a plaintext password.
  4. Routing by database name. The name in the startup packet picks a line of the generated databases.ini: the backend host and port, the backend database, and pool limits. PgBouncer connects to the backend as the same user and passes SCRAM through.
  5. The backend. One of three things: the shared cluster or dedicated instance that holds the database; the read replicas, for <db>_ro; or, for a paused or archived Free project, the waker.

There is no SNI routing and no per-project hostname for Postgres. A region has one hostname and one certificate, and the database name alone picks the project. The data API, auth, storage and realtime go through xenibase-edge instead, which does route by hostname.

The generated files

xenibase-server owns three files in the pooler directory (XENIBASE_POOLER_CONFIG_DIR, mounted read-only into each PgBouncer at /etc/pgbouncer/xenibase). Render produces them from a Config of routes, users and restrictions. Entries are sorted, so the same input gives byte-identical files. Names are validated, never escaped, so a bad name upstream cannot inject configuration:

FileOne line perExample
databases.iniRoute: the project's database, its V1 alias if it has one, and <db>_ro if it has read replicasblog_k2f9 = host=10.0.0.21 port=5432 dbname=blog_k2f9 pool_size=15 max_db_connections=60
userlist.txtLogin: owner, read-only login, members' personal logins, probe, edge and request-role logins, logins an owner created with role management, and the static admin user"blog_k2f9_owner" "SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:…"
hba.confAllowlist rule, then the defaulthost all all 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256

Manager.Sync builds one Config per region under a Postgres advisory lock, so two servers never interleave. It reads projects in a live status whose organisation is not suspended (PoolerRoutes; a suspended organisation simply loses its routes), their replicas, and every kind of login. A project is routed by its region's poolers, or by the home region's when its region has no pooler hosts. For 30 days after a move it is also routed by its old region's, so old connection strings keep working. A region's files go in the main directory for the home region, regions/<id>/ for the others. Files are written atomically (temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync) in a fixed order: users, then hba.conf, then routes. A new route is never served before its user can log in, or wider than its allowlist. Then every pooler gets RELOAD (distribute).

The admin console also carries PAUSE/RESUME around cutovers, KILL for deletes and password rotations, and RECONNECT. Freeze pauses the transaction pooler, falling back to KILL after a wait, and kills on the session pooler, whose clients would otherwise hold PAUSE open. Each command goes only to the poolers that route that database.

One project's login on another's database

PgBouncer has no notion of which login belongs to which route. Any user in userlist.txt may ask for any database in databases.ini, and PgBouncer will open a backend connection as that user. Isolation is the backend's job: every project database has REVOKE ALL … FROM PUBLIC and CONNECT granted to its own roles only (ensureDatabase), so Postgres refuses the login. isocheck verifies that nightly on every cluster. The auth file is also one namespace per region, so login names must be unique across projects. Logins an owner creates must be named <db>_…, may not be one of the project's or Xenibase's own names (platformRole), and lose to a platform login of the same name.

The per-project IP allowlist

New in v4.2.4 (migration 00058). PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/network stores up to 50 networks in projects.allowed_cidrs. NormalizeAllowedCIDRs turns bare addresses into /32 or /128, unmaps IPv4-in-IPv6, and refuses host bits, zones and /0. A check constraint repeats the limit of 50.

For each project with a list, renderHBA writes its rules ahead of the default. PgBouncer takes the first line that matches:

The databases are the project's name, its _ro route and its V1 alias, so neither port nor any route is left open. Both PgBouncers read the same file. The exempt logins (Platform) are the five backend-service logins and the SLA probe. Their passwords never leave Xenibase, and the API keys and row-level security protect what they can do. The dashboard's SQL editor, backups, moves and HA connect to instances directly, not through the poolers. Provisioning and password rotation skip their own connect-through-the-pooler smoke test while a list exists, because it would come from the server's address.

Risk
  • Nothing checks that it is enforced. The agent writes hba.conf whatever PgBouncer's auth_type is. A pooler host still on the pre-4.2.4 pgbouncer.ini (auth_type = scram-sha-256) ignores the file and reports ready, so a list is stored and shown but not applied. The upgrade notes say to upgrade pooler hosts first, but the arbiter could check: SHOW CONFIG on the admin console it already uses.
  • It covers the poolers only. Instances accept SCRAM logins from every private range (XENIBASE_AGENT_DB_ALLOW). Anything on the private network with the password, such as a dedicated project's postgres_fdw, is not subject to the list.
  • The final host all all 0.0.0.0/0 rule also admits the admin console (database pgbouncer, user xenibase) from the internet, with only its password in the way. A rule limiting pgbouncer to the private network would cost nothing.
Resolved

The allowlist could be bypassed through an import, which connected from xenibase-server and an agent straight to any address the caller named. An import's source is now checked and pinned, and Xenibase's own addresses are refused. See Nodes and agents.

Note

The poolers see the address a connection arrives from. PROXY protocol is not used anywhere: pooler hosts run with host networking behind a floating IP, which keeps the source address. In the compose bundle, Docker's port publishing keeps it for IPv4, but an IPv6 client reached through docker-proxy arrives from the bridge gateway (172.31.250.1) and is refused by any list that does not name that address.

Pooler hosts, keepalived and the floating IP

With pooler hosts (V3 §2.1) each region has two machines. Each runs both PgBouncers and the agent in pooler mode in one container, and keepalived in another, the only one with NET_ADMIN (deploy/pooler-host).

Getting the files there

After writing the files, pushHosts reads each region's bundle. That is its three files plus the TLS pair: the region's own if it has one, else the main directory's (readBundle). It hashes the bundle, advances the region's generation in the metadata database, and sends PUT /v1/pooler/config to each of the region's hosts over the agent's mutual TLS. Then it tells every host the generation, including any that just failed. A push fails only when every host refuses it. A host that missed it knows it is stale.

The agent accepts only the five known file names, requires the routes and auth file, checks the hash against the content, and refuses an older generation with 409 (two servers raced). It writes users, rules, key, certificate, then routes, and sends SIGHUP to the PgBouncers (apply). The generation served and the generation expected are kept in a state file, so they survive a restart.

Who holds the address

A host is ready when it has a configuration, serves the newest generation the server has announced, and both PgBouncers accept TCP connections (status). keepalived asks the agent's loopback /ready every second. Two failures drop the host out, and unicast VRRP with one-second adverts hands over in about 3 to 4 seconds. Both hosts start as BACKUP with nopreempt, so a host that comes back does not take the address back (keepalived.conf). keepalived's notify posts the new state to the agent. On MASTER the agent asks Hetzner to route the floating IP to its own server, retrying with backoff for up to two minutes, and stops when the state changes (setVRRP).

xenibase-server's arbiter checks each region's pair every 3 seconds. It re-pushes to a stale host, at most every 15 seconds, and asks Hetzner where the IP points. Its rule is Decide:

It moves the IP only after the holder has been unhealthy for two checks in a row, so keepalived's own move goes first. Each move, change of holder, split brain, host going stale and recovery is recorded as a pooler event and shown in Admin → Nodes.

Split brain

If the two hosts lose sight of each other but not of Hetzner, both become MASTER. Both agents then assign the IP once. Assign is a no-op when the IP already points at the caller. The last assignment wins, and neither agent claims again until its state changes. The arbiter reports split_brain but leaves a healthy holder alone, so nothing flaps. Both hosts are stateless and serve the same generation, so whichever receives the traffic routes it correctly. A host that missed a change cannot be ready, so cannot hold the address through keepalived. Two cases remain. If the control plane cannot reach the holder, the arbiter moves the address after six seconds even though clients could still reach it. That is a needless failover, not a wrong one. And while the control plane is down, nothing announces new generations, so a host that missed the last push before the outage still counts as ready.

Risk

Each pooler host holds a Hetzner Cloud API token with read and write access (XENIBASE_AGENT_HETZNER_TOKEN), because the agent assigns the floating IP itself. Hetzner tokens cannot be narrowed to one IP. Pooler hosts are the only machines that face the internet on a database port, and a compromise of one hands over every server, volume and network in the Hetzner project, database nodes included. Leaving assignment to xenibase-server, which already moves the address, or putting a narrow proxy in front of the API would keep the token off them, at the cost of a slower failover when the control plane is down.

Spec and code differ

V3 §2.1 says the server "verifies both hashes match". Staleness is decided by generation. The agent checks each bundle's hash against its content, and the server records each host's hash, but nothing compares the two hosts' hashes.

TLS for the database hostname

internal/tlscert keeps server.crt and server.key in the pooler directory for the database hostname (Settings → DB hostname). It has four modes (XENIBASE_POOLER_TLS):

ModeCertificate
acme (bundle default)Let's Encrypt or another ACME CA through certmagic, HTTP-01 only. Caddy forwards /.well-known/acme-challenge/ to the server. A self-signed certificate stands in until the first issue, and whenever the hostname is an IP or not a public name (acmeable).
self-signedP-256, one year, replaced when it has less than 30 days left or no longer names the host.
filesOperator-supplied PEM files, copied in.
offNothing is written.

ensure runs at start, on a hostname change, twice a day, and after a failure with backoff up to an hour. It checks that the pair matches and writes the key before the certificate, then reloads the poolers, which pushes the pair to pooler hosts. Clients are told to use sslmode=require, which encrypts but does not check the certificate. verify-full works when the certificate is from a public CA.

Risk
  • A region's own pooler hostname never gets a certificate. Regions have their own hostname (regions.pooler_host, for example db.ng.example.com), but the server builds one tlscert.Manager, for the home hostname (setupPoolerTLS). Nothing writes a pair into regions/<id>/, so readBundle always falls back to the home pair. Clients of a non-home region that use verify-full fail on the hostname. With require, nothing protects them from an impostor.
  • The hops behind the poolers are not verified. PgBouncer connects to backends with server_tls_sslmode = prefer, so it falls back to plain text and never checks a certificate. That is reasonable on one private network, but not for routes that cross regions: a region without its own poolers is served from the home region, and a moved project is forwarded from its old one for 30 days. The edge connects to the poolers with sslmode=require by default (XENIBASE_EDGE_POOLER_SSLMODE), as the service logins. Someone in the path cannot learn the password from SCRAM, but can take over the session after it.
Spec and code differ

V1 §3.3 has the pooler certificate "obtained via DNS-01 or HTTP-01". The pooler certificate is HTTP-01 only (TLS-ALPN is turned off, and there is no DNS-01 solver in tlscert). DNS-01 exists for the edge's wildcard, outside this package.

The waker

A Free project that sits idle is paused, and later archived (V3 §4.2–§4.3). Its route then points at the waker instead of its cluster, with pool_size and max_db_connections of 1:

The waker (internal/waker) runs inside xenibase-server on XENIBASE_WAKER_LISTEN. It speaks just enough of the protocol to answer. It declines TLS and GSS, reads the startup packet (at most 10,000 bytes, three tries), and asks freetier.Wake to queue a resume or an unarchive. A request while another operation runs on the project is a no-op. It then closes the connection with a FATAL error that says what is happening (Code):

ProjectSQLSTATEThe client sees
Paused08004"…paused for inactivity and is resuming. Retry in about 30 seconds."
Archived08004"…being restored from its archive. Retry in a few minutes."
Already active (the route is about to switch back)57P03, which PgBouncer treats as a server starting and holds the client"Retry in a few seconds."
Unknown database3D000"This database is not available."

A connection storm is bounded three times. Each PgBouncer opens at most one server connection per paused database. The waker handles at most 256 connections at once, and refuses the rest at accept with 53300, without waking anything. Each connection has a 10-second deadline, and its wake call half of that. The wake itself is one locked row and an idempotent enqueue.

Risk

The waker does not authenticate. It relies on PgBouncer having checked the client's password first, and on listening "on an address only the poolers reach". The bundle listens on :6435 inside its Docker network. With pooler hosts elsewhere it must listen where they can reach it, and nothing restricts the source. Anyone who reaches it can wake any paused project, or start an archived project's restore, by sending its database name in a startup packet. The edge does the same for any request to a paused project's hostname, before the API key is checked, limited to once per 30 seconds per edge (wake). The cost is compute and archive restores rather than data. Checking the source address against the pooler hosts, and the key before waking, would close both.

xenibase-edge

xenibase-edge (cmd/edge) serves each project's backend services at https://<ref>.<domain>. The data API, auth, storage and realtime are described in Part D. This section covers how it connects.

The configuration feed

The edge keeps every project's configuration in memory and gets it from xenibase-server. It long-polls GET /api/v1/edge/config?since=…&wait=25 for changes and reads the whole feed again every minute as a backstop (apply ignores an older version that a resync brings back). An entry carries the pooler database and address, the edge login's and the request roles' passwords, the hashes of live API keys, the JWT verification keys, CORS, rate and cache settings, and the state. disabled removes the project. A project's database pools are kept while its connection details are unchanged, and closed when they change. Until the first full read the edge answers 503.

Every call in either direction carries Xenibase-Signature, an HMAC-SHA256 over the time, method, request URI and body with the shared edge secret. The receiver accepts five minutes of clock difference (edgeapi.Verify).

Risk

There is one edge secret for the whole platform (XENIBASE_EDGE_SECRET). The region an edge serves is a query parameter the edge chooses (Config). An empty one means all regions. So a regional edge, and the cloud-init of every edge node Xenibase creates, holds a key that reads every project's service-role password in every region. That weakens the point of a data-residency region having its own edge. A secret per edge, bound to its region on the server, would contain a compromise to one region.

From hostname to transaction

  1. refFromHost takes the HTTP Host, lower-cased, without port or trailing dot. It must be exactly one label in front of XENIBASE_EDGE_DOMAIN. The edge serves a wildcard certificate whatever the SNI says, and the Host header alone picks the project.
  2. authorize looks the apikey up by its SHA-256 among that project's keys only. A key from another project is simply not found, so a Host header cannot be used to point one project's key at another. A secret key means the service role, and is refused from a browser unless the project allows it. A publishable key means anon, or user with a bearer token. The token must verify against that project's own ES256 keys with the project's ref as audience, and carry role: user. Per-IP and per-key limits apply. The client address is the RemoteAddr, or the last X-Forwarded-For entry when the peer is in XENIBASE_EDGE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (clientIP).
  3. WithRequest runs the whole request in one transaction through the transaction pooler, as the role's own login (<db>_anon, _user, _service), with the claims and statement timeout set with set_config(…, true). Nothing outlives the transaction, so transaction pooling is safe, and tenant SQL that resets the role stays that role. Only a feed from a server older than M32, which has no request-role passwords, makes the edge log in as the edge login and SET LOCAL ROLE.

Pools are small: four connections per login, two for the service and hook roles. They use pgx's exec mode, with no server-side prepared statements kept between transactions (loginPool). GETs that may read from replicas use the <db>_ro route. These logins are the ones exempt from IP allowlists. The Bloom filter in internal/bloom sends a project's counted monthly users to the edge in a few kilobytes. A false positive lets an uncounted user in.
